p: Malibu is twenty-one miles of coastline and, in effect, one road. The Pacific Coast Highway runs the length of it with the ocean on one side and the Santa Monica Mountains rising steeply on the other, and everything here — the houses, the beaches, the canyons, the traffic, the fires — follows from that geometry. There is no downtown. There is a string of beaches, canyons, coves and small commercial clusters strung along a single highway between Santa Monica and the Ventura County line.

What that produces is one of the most beautiful residential coastlines in the world and one of the most constrained. The mountains behind are almost entirely national recreation area and state park; the coast in front is regulated by one of the strictest coastal planning regimes in the United States; and the city itself, incorporated only in 1991, has spent its entire existence resisting development. The practical consequence is a supply of housing that is essentially fixed, on a coast within an hour of eighteen million people.

For a buyer, the honest framing is this. Malibu offers a quality of setting — ocean, mountains, light, surf, canyon trails from the door — that very few places on earth match, with a great city forty-five minutes east. It also carries a set of risks that are real, current and must be understood rather than glossed over: wildfire, the single highway, coastal erosion, and an insurance market that has become genuinely difficult. This guide spends more time on those than a listing would, because in Malibu they are not footnotes. They are part of what you are buying.

sections.h: A short history: from Humaliwo to the highway
p: The Chumash lived along this coast for thousands of years; the name Malibu descends from their village name at the lagoon, generally translated as something close to 'the surf sounds loudly', which remains the most accurate description of the place anyone has managed. Spanish and then Mexican land grants turned the coast into a single vast ranch, and in 1892 that ranch was bought whole by a wealthy Massachusetts family.

What happened next explains the modern coastline. The family — and after her husband's death, May Rindge in particular — fought for decades to keep the ranch private and roadless, building a private railway to block a public one and litigating all the way to the United States Supreme Court to stop a highway being pushed through. She lost. The Pacific Coast Highway opened in 1929, and Malibu was opened with it. To raise money during the fight she had begun leasing beachfront lots to Hollywood people, which created the Malibu Colony and set the coast's social character for the next century.

The rest followed quickly: the surf culture that grew up at the point beside the pier in the 1950s and 1960s and effectively invented modern longboarding and the beach-movie era; the canyon houses and the counterculture of the 1960s and 1970s; the university on the hill; and the steady accumulation of very expensive houses on very exposed land. The city incorporated in 1991, largely in order to control its own planning. And through all of it runs the constant of this coast — fire, flood and slide — which has shaped Malibu's history at least as much as any of its residents have.

East Malibu, from the county line at Topanga to the pier, is the closest to Los Angeles and the most urban stretch: Carbon Beach and the tight run of beachfront houses along it, Malibu Colony behind its gate, the Malibu Pier, the lagoon and Surfrider Beach beside it, and the Country Mart shopping cluster which functions as the closest thing Malibu has to a town centre. Fastest access to Santa Monica and the city; most traffic.

Central Malibu runs from the pier out past Pepperdine's hillside campus to Point Dume. This is where the canyons open — Malibu Canyon, Latigo, Corral — and where a great deal of the residential hillside sits, with houses looking down the coast. Paradise Cove and its beach café are along here, as is Escondido Canyon with its waterfall walk.

Point Dume is the headland that divides the coast, and the neighbourhood behind it — a grid of streets on the bluff with deeded beach access rights for residents — is one of the most sought-after addresses in Malibu. Westward Beach below it and Zuma Beach immediately north are the great wide sands of this coast, and the point itself is a state preserve with whale watching in the migration seasons.

West Malibu runs from Zuma out to the county line: Broad Beach, Trancas with its market and restaurants, then the wilder end — El Matador, La Piedra and El Pescador, the pocket beaches beneath the bluffs with sea stacks and caves that are the most photographed shoreline in southern California. Beyond them, Leo Carrillo, the state park, and the county line where the surf shack at the end of the road has been selling fish and chips to surfers for decades. This is the quietest, greenest, least crowded part of Malibu — and the furthest from anything.

sections.h: Where exactly to own: micro-locations, rated
p: Beachfront. The Malibu proposition in its purest form: the ocean beneath the deck and sand at the bottom of the steps. The most expensive land on the coast, and the most exposed — to storm surf, to erosion, and to the highest insurance costs. Also, in some stretches, to the public's right of access across the wet sand, which is a genuine and occasionally contentious feature of California law.

Point Dume. The connoisseur's neighbourhood: a bluff-top grid of streets with big lots, mature landscaping, ocean views and — for residents — deeded access down to the beach below. Quiet, family-oriented, and about as close to a settled residential neighbourhood as Malibu offers.

The bluffs and hillsides. Houses above the highway with the whole coast laid out below them, from modest to extraordinary. Views are the product, and they are genuinely extraordinary. The trades are access up narrow roads, greater wildfire exposure than the beachfront, and — on some parcels — geological questions worth investigating properly.

The canyons. Malibu Canyon, Latigo, Corral, Zuma and the others: oak and sycamore, creeks, seclusion, cooler air, and trailheads at the door. Materially better value than the coast, a genuinely different lifestyle, and the highest wildfire exposure on this list — which is a sentence to take seriously rather than as a formality.

West Malibu and Trancas. The quiet end: Zuma and Broad Beach, the Trancas market and restaurants, the pocket beaches, and the state parks beyond. Better value than the east, more space, and thirty to forty minutes further from Los Angeles — which for many owners is the point.

Just beyond: Ventura County. Over the county line the coast continues past Neptune's Net towards Oxnard, with dramatically lower prices and the same ocean. Worth a look for buyers who want the coast more than the postcode.

sections.h: Wildfire and insurance: what to check
p: Malibu sits in a wildland-urban interface in a Mediterranean climate with autumn offshore winds, and fire is part of this coast's history. The Woolsey Fire in November 2018 swept from the Santa Monica Mountains to the sea and destroyed a large number of structures across the area; in January 2025 a fire in the Palisades area burned west into eastern Malibu. These are recent events, and they shape how a purchase here should be approached — not as a reason to avoid the coast, which people have owned and loved for a century, but as the first question to answer rather than the last.

The consequences for an owner are practical and ongoing. Insurance is the sharp end: carriers have withdrawn from or repriced high-fire-risk areas across California, the state's insurer of last resort has taken on a far larger role than intended, and premiums in Malibu are very high and rising. Cover must be confirmed for the specific property before commitment — not assumed, not estimated. In some cases the availability of cover, rather than its price, is the binding constraint.

Beyond insurance: defensible-space requirements around homes are enforced and consequential; wildland-interface building standards for new and rebuilt construction — ember-resistant venting, non-combustible roofing and cladding, tempered glazing — materially change both risk and insurability, so a recently rebuilt house is a different proposition from a 1970s one; and the post-fire hazard is not over when the fire is out, because burned slopes shed debris flows in the following winter rains, which have historically closed the highway and damaged property below.

Handled properly, all of this is manageable — and it is exactly the kind of thing a professionally managed, shared home handles better than an absent single owner, because brush clearance, compliance, insurance administration and fire-season preparation happen whether or not anyone is in residence. What it means in practice is that the fire question sits at the centre of choosing a property rather than at the edge: the parcel's exposure, the construction standard, the defensible space and the current insurance position. We check all of it on every home we list and tell you plainly what we find — and where we cannot get comfortable, we do not list the home.

sections.h: The highway, the slides and getting about
p: Malibu has one road. The Pacific Coast Highway runs the length of the city and there is no parallel route; the canyon roads over the mountains to the San Fernando Valley are the only alternatives, and they are winding, slow and themselves subject to closure. This is the second structural fact about living here after the fire risk, and it deserves the same honesty.

In ordinary conditions the highway is simply a beautiful drive that gets busy: summer weekends, beach traffic, and the eastbound commute towards Santa Monica all slow it. Owners learn the hours. In extraordinary conditions — storm surf, rockfall, debris flow after a fire, a wildfire itself, or a serious collision — the highway closes, sometimes for hours and occasionally for much longer, and when it does there is no way around. Anyone whose plans depend on being somewhere at a particular time should build that into their thinking.

The practical driving numbers, in good conditions: Santa Monica twenty-five to thirty-five minutes from east Malibu; downtown Los Angeles about an hour; Los Angeles International Airport forty-five minutes to an hour and a quarter depending on traffic and on where in Malibu you are; Burbank sometimes easier. From west Malibu add twenty to thirty minutes to all of it. A car is essential; there is no meaningful public transport and nothing is walkable except within each small commercial cluster.

sections.h: The beaches, the surf and the water
p: Malibu's beaches are its glory and they are more varied than the postcards suggest. Zuma is the great wide sand — long, clean, lifeguarded, with room for everyone, and the default family beach. Westward, immediately south beneath Point Dume, is smaller and more sheltered. Surfrider, beside the pier, is the historic one: a right-hand point break that shaped modern longboard surfing in the 1950s and 1960s and was designated the world's first World Surfing Reserve. It is crowded, competitive and worth watching even if you never paddle out.

The pocket beaches at the western end — El Matador above all — are the photographed ones: sea stacks, arches and caves beneath steep bluffs, reached by stairs, and at their best in the last hour of light. Paradise Cove has a beach café that has been there for decades. Leo Carrillo at the county line has tide pools and campgrounds. Access to all of them is public, and California law protects the public's right to the wet sand even in front of private houses — a principle that has been litigated repeatedly along this coast and is worth understanding as a fact of ownership here.

In the water: surfing at every level and every point along the coast; kayaking and paddleboarding out of the coves; diving and snorkelling around Point Dume; whale watching from the headland in the migration seasons, with grey whales in winter and spring and, increasingly, humpbacks and blue whales offshore in summer; and dolphins more or less constantly. Water temperature is Californian — a wetsuit extends the season considerably, and most people here own one.

The half of Malibu that visitors miss is uphill. The Santa Monica Mountains rise directly behind the coast and are almost entirely protected as national recreation area, state park and conservancy land — which is why the ridgelines are empty and why the supply of buildable land is what it is. For an owner this is an enormous amenity: hundreds of miles of trail beginning at the top of the canyons, five minutes from the highway.

The obvious walks. Solstice Canyon, an easy shaded loop past a ruined house and a waterfall. Escondido Falls, the highest waterfall in the range, up a canyon from the highway. Point Dume's headland loop for the whale watching. Malibu Creek State Park, inland through the canyon, with a gorge, a lake and the meadow where a long-running television series was filmed. Sandstone Peak, the highest point in the mountains at a little over three thousand feet, with a view from the ocean to the valley on a clear day. And running through all of it, the long-distance trail that traverses the entire range from Los Angeles to the county line.

The canyons are also the region's cycling: Latigo, Piuma, Stunt and Mulholland are famous climbs, and the coast road is a classic ride when the traffic allows. In spring, after a wet winter, the hills go green and the wildflowers are exceptional. The honest counterpart, again, is that this same landscape is the fuel load that makes the fire risk what it is — the beauty and the hazard are the same thing seen from different angles.

sections.h: A year on the coast, month by month
p: January and February are cool, often bright, and the wettest months of a not-very-wet year — this is when the hills go green and the creeks run. Grey whales pass offshore. It is the quietest the coast gets and, for owners who like an empty beach and a fire in the evening, among the best times to be here. March and April bring the green hills at their peak and the wildflowers in the mountains; the walking is at its finest and the beaches are still empty.

May and June carry the coastal cloud that southern California names after those months: mornings often grey, burning off by early afternoon, with the water still cold. It is a lovely, quiet time inland and a slightly disappointing one on the sand. July and August are the summer proper — warm, dry, busy, with the highway slow at weekends, the beaches full and the water at its most swimmable.

September and October are the best months of the year: warm, clear, the ocean at its warmest, the crowds gone after the first week of September, and the light turning gold. They are also the heart of the offshore-wind season, when fire risk is at its highest — the two facts sit together and both are true. November brings the first rains in a normal year, cooler air and a quiet coast; December is mild, green and often beautiful. There is no unusable month here; there is only a coast that is busiest in July and at its best in October.

Malibu has no town centre, so its everyday life happens in a handful of commercial clusters strung along the highway. The Country Mart and the Village at the eastern end hold the largest concentration: a grocery, restaurants, cafés, shops and a bookshop, arranged around courtyards, and functioning as the closest thing the city has to a high street. Trancas Country Market at the western end does a smaller version, with a market, a couple of good restaurants and a pharmacy.

The restaurants are a mixture of the internationally famous, the long-established and the pleasantly ordinary: a celebrated Japanese restaurant on the water at the eastern end that requires planning, a beach café at Paradise Cove that requires none, a clifftop institution or two, a fish shack at the county line that surfers have eaten at for decades, and a good layer of cafés and taquerias in between. Prices at the top end are Los Angeles prices with a view premium.

For anything more, you drive: Santa Monica and Pacific Palisades to the east have the full range of shops, restaurants and services, and Los Angeles beyond them. The practical shape of a week here is a large shop done on the way in, most meals cooked at home on a deck looking at the ocean, and two or three meals out — which is not a compromise, because in Malibu the house and its view are the point rather than the restaurants.

Malibu is a straightforwardly good place for children, with one significant caveat about the road. The assets: Zuma Beach, which is wide, clean, lifeguarded and gentle enough for small children with room to run; Westward and Paradise Cove for calmer water; tide pools at Leo Carrillo; the canyon walks, which are short, shaded and have waterfalls at the end of them; and the simple business of a house with a garden above the sea.

Beyond that: surf lessons, which this coast does better than anywhere; kayaking and paddleboarding in the coves; the whale migration in winter and spring, visible from the headland; horse riding in the canyons; and the Getty Villa at the eastern edge, a recreated Roman villa full of antiquities that is free to visit and unexpectedly gripping for older children. Los Angeles's museums, the aquarium at Long Beach and the theme parks are all within reach for a day.

The caveat is the highway. It is fast, busy and runs between most houses and most beaches; children cannot cycle to the sand and crossing it on foot needs care and a marked crossing. That shapes how a family week works here — it is a driving-and-house holiday rather than a wandering one. For ownership groups the calendar is easy: this coast is at its best in September and October, so families take July and August while everyone else takes the shoulders, and the rotation has little to arbitrate.

East, the city. Santa Monica is twenty-five to thirty-five minutes with its pier, promenade and restaurants. Beyond it, Los Angeles in all its forms: the Getty Center on its hill, the county art museum, the Broad, Griffith Observatory, the food of every culture on earth, and a music and theatre calendar that runs continuously. An hour's drive puts a world city at your disposal, which is a great deal more than most beautiful coastlines can say.

Inland, over the canyons, the San Fernando Valley and beyond it the studios, the Hollywood Bowl in summer, and the route north into the mountains. Malibu Creek State Park sits in the middle of the range with a gorge and a lake. And the Santa Monica Mountains' own trail network, described above, is a day out in itself.

West and north, the coast keeps going: Ventura and the Channel Islands, from which boats run to a national park of largely uninhabited islands with extraordinary sea life; Ojai, an hour and a half inland, a small town in a valley of orange groves with a particular light at sunset that locals have named; Santa Barbara at about ninety minutes, which is the most beautiful small city in California; and the wine country of the Santa Ynez valley beyond it. A Malibu house is a base for the whole of southern California's coast, not just for one stretch of it.

Malibu is one of the most expensive residential markets in the United States and the reasons are structural. Supply is fixed by geography and by regulation: the mountains behind are protected land, the coast in front is governed by California's coastal regime, which makes new development on the shoreline extremely difficult, and the city's own planning has been consistently restrictive since incorporation. Demand comes from Los Angeles — one of the largest concentrations of wealth on earth, forty-five minutes away — and from an international buyer pool.

The gradient runs by frontage and by view. Beachfront commands the highest premium, followed by bluff-top with ocean views, then hillside view property, then canyon and inland. Point Dume and the Colony are the established prestige neighbourhoods. West Malibu offers more space for less. Recently built or rebuilt houses carry a substantial premium over older stock, and here that is about far more than finishes — current wildland-interface construction standards materially affect both risk and insurability.

Four specifics belong in any honest account, and they are more consequential here than almost anywhere. First, insurance: expensive, difficult and in some cases hard to obtain at all; it must be confirmed for the specific property before commitment, and it may be the binding constraint on a purchase. Second, wildfire exposure, which varies enormously by parcel — canyon and hillside positions are not the same risk as an oceanfront lot. Third, the coastal permitting regime, which governs what can be built, rebuilt or altered and is genuinely slow and strict. Fourth, wastewater: much of Malibu has historically been on onsite systems rather than mains sewer, and the applicable requirements are a real due-diligence item on many parcels.

For a share buyer, the arithmetic in Malibu is as favourable as anywhere on our books. These are large, expensive houses carrying very high fixed costs — insurance above all — for properties that a single household uses a handful of weeks a year. Sharing spreads exactly the costs that make Malibu difficult, and it puts a house on this coast within reach of households for whom whole ownership here would never be sensible.

Four supports, and they are strong. First, absolute scarcity: twenty-one miles of coast with protected mountains behind and a coastal regulator in front. The stock of Malibu houses is essentially fixed and, if anything, shrinks. Second, the setting itself — ocean, mountains, light and surf in a combination that has no substitute within a thousand miles, and a global recognition factor that few addresses possess.

Third, Los Angeles: a vast and wealthy metropolitan economy forty-five minutes east, with an entertainment, technology and finance base that has sustained demand for this coast for a century. Fourth, the length of the usable year — this is a twelve-month climate, best in September and October, entirely pleasant in January.

The things to weigh against them: wildfire risk that has produced two major events in recent memory; an insurance market that is expensive and in places unavailable; a single highway subject to closure; coastal erosion and post-fire debris flow; and a permitting environment that makes any building work slow. These are not reasons the market falls — it has absorbed all of them repeatedly — but they are reasons that buying here requires more diligence than buying almost anywhere else, and reasons that the running costs of a Malibu house are higher than an equivalent elsewhere. Which is precisely the case for sharing them.

Malibu's ownership is famous at the top and much more ordinary beneath it. The best-known layer is the entertainment and business wealth that has been buying on this coast since the Colony was first leased in the 1920s, concentrated on the beachfront and at Point Dume. Below that sits a large and long-established community of people who bought before the market ran: surfers, artists, teachers, canyon families, and second and third generations of the same households.

There is a genuine year-round population with schools, a university on the hill, churches, a farmers' market and a fiercely engaged local politics — Malibu is a city that argues with itself about development, roads, sewers and wildfire policy at considerable volume, and a new owner does well to arrive with some humility about that. There is also, unavoidably, a large seasonal and part-time layer.

For a co-owner the practical consequence is a coast entirely accustomed to houses that are occupied part of the time, with a mature property management, caretaking and maintenance industry — and, importantly here, professional handling of the things that matter most: brush clearance and defensible-space compliance, insurance administration, storm and fire-season preparation, and the systems maintenance that a house on this coast demands. A house used by several households in rotation is unremarkable; a house on this coast left unattended is a genuine liability.

Buyers looking at the southern Californian coast compare a short list. Against Santa Barbara and Montecito, ninety minutes north: arguably more beautiful, more town, more genteel, with its own fire history and comparable prices — and a good deal further from Los Angeles. Against Newport Beach and Laguna, ninety minutes south: a harbour, an airport fifteen minutes away, calmer geography and much lower fire exposure, with less drama in the landscape. Against the Palisades and Santa Monica: closer to the city, more urban, less coast.

Against Europe, for a European buyer: the Mediterranean is cheaper, closer and warm in the northern summer; Malibu is warm all year and at its best in autumn. As with the other Californian and Floridian addresses on our list, it works best as a complement to a European property rather than a replacement.

Malibu's own case, stated plainly: twenty-one miles of some of the most beautiful coastline in the world, with protected mountains behind it and hundreds of miles of trail from the canyon tops; the birthplace of modern surf culture; a twelve-month climate that peaks in October; and Los Angeles forty-five minutes east. The things to weigh are the ones set out above — fire exposure, insurance and a single highway — and they are worth resolving early rather than late. For buyers who do that work, there is nothing quite like this coast.

Here is how a share of a home here actually works. You buy a deeded fraction of a specific, fully furnished, professionally managed property — real property, recorded in your name, which you can sell, pass on or hold. It is not a timeshare, not a points scheme and not a club membership: your interest tracks the value of that specific home in the local market. The calendar allocates usage fairly across the owners, rotating the contested dates — the summer weeks, Thanksgiving, the Christmas period, the September and October shoulder that Malibu regulars prize most — from year to year so no owner is permanently advantaged, with flexible booking for everything else.

Malibu is the clearest cost case on our books after Aspen, and for a different reason: it is not only the purchase price. The recurring costs of a house on this coast — insurance above all, plus brush clearance and defensible-space compliance, wastewater system maintenance, salt-air upkeep, storm and fire-season preparation — are high and rising, and a single household carries all of them for a house used six or eight weeks a year. Sharing spreads precisely the costs that make Malibu difficult, which is a stronger argument here than in most places.

The management case is equally strong and more urgent. A house on this coast left unattended between visits is a liability: brush grows, systems fail, salt air corrodes, and fire season requires active preparation rather than hope. Professional management handles compliance, preparation, inspection, cleaning between stays and the vendor relationships that matter when an entire coast needs the same trade at the same time.

Costs are shared in the same proportion as ownership: each owner carries their share of the home's running costs, billed transparently, covering property taxes, insurance, utilities, landscaping and brush clearance, wastewater and systems maintenance, cleaning, maintenance and the reserve that keeps the furnishings good. You see the full breakdown before you buy, not after — and in Malibu, the insurance line is the one to read first.

sections.h: Buying in the United States: how the process actually runs
p: American property transactions run differently from European ones and are, once understood, fast and well-supported. There is no notary in the civil-law sense. In California the transaction runs through an escrow company and a title insurer: escrow holds the deposit and coordinates the closing, while the title company researches the chain of title, resolves liens and issues title insurance protecting the buyer against defects missed in the search. That insurance is standard and one of the real strengths of the system.

The sequence: an offer on a standard state-approved contract; a contingency period during which the buyer inspects, reviews disclosures and can generally withdraw; title and disclosure review; and closing, typically within thirty to sixty days. California's disclosure regime is thorough, with natural-hazard reports covering fire, flood and seismic zones as standard. In Malibu, the contingency period is where the real work happens, and it should be used properly: insurance quotes obtained and confirmed in writing before you commit; the parcel's fire hazard severity zone; geological and drainage reports on hillside and canyon lots; coastal permit history and any restrictions on rebuilding or altering; the wastewater system and its compliance status; and, on beachfront, the erosion and sea-wall position.

There is no restriction on foreign ownership of American residential property. Non-US buyers will need a taxpayer identification number for filing purposes, should expect withholding rules to apply on a future sale, and should take advice on how their home country treats US-situs assets — including estate and inheritance treatment, the point most often overlooked at this price level. For a co-ownership share, the structure is prepared once, professionally, and each buyer steps into it. We walk every buyer through the specimen documents in plain language before any commitment, and we will always encourage independent legal and tax advice. Nothing in this guide is legal or tax advice.

Three honest specimen years. The family: a week at Easter when the hills are green, a fortnight in July and August built around Zuma, the surf lessons and the canyon walks, a long weekend at Thanksgiving, and a few days after Christmas. Six-plus weeks in a house that already holds the boards, the wetsuits and the beach kit.

The couple who know the coast: ten days in late September and early October, which is the best fortnight of the Malibu year — warm water, empty beaches, gold light — plus a week in April for the wildflowers and the walking, a long weekend in January for the whales and an empty beach, and a few days in June inland when the coast is grey and the canyons are not. A calendar assembled almost entirely from weeks nobody competes for, and better than the peak ones.

The friends' syndicate: alternating long weekends through the spring and autumn — a surf, a canyon walk, a dinner at the Country Mart, a day in the city — plus one shared summer week when the households and children combine, and a standing Getty-and-museums day each visit. Three shapes, one common property: on a coast with a twelve-month climate and Los Angeles forty-five minutes away, six weeks a year is not a constraint to be managed. It is a budget to be spent well.

The small knowledge that makes ownership frictionless, and here some of it is safety rather than convenience. Fire season: from late summer through autumn, when offshore winds blow, keep a packed bag, know your evacuation route, sign up for the county's emergency alerts, and take warnings seriously and early rather than late. Do not wait to see. The management team handles brush clearance and seasonal preparation, but evacuation decisions are yours and they are best made quickly.

The highway: check conditions before you set out, particularly in winter after a fire year, when debris flows close it. Allow more time than the map suggests on summer weekends and in the eastbound morning. There is no alternative route, so build a margin into flights and appointments.

The coast: the surf here is bigger and stronger than it looks, rip currents are real, and lifeguarded beaches exist for a reason. Water is cool enough that a wetsuit extends the season considerably, particularly for children. Sun at this latitude is serious year-round.

The house: salt air is hard on metal, timber and glass, and a coastal house needs continuous rather than occasional attention. Brush clearance is a legal obligation with real consequences. Wastewater systems need servicing. All of it is handled by the management team, which is one of the concrete reasons an unmanaged Malibu house declines quickly. And the golden rule: whatever week you cannot use, release it early — in a place forty-five minutes from four million people, someone in your ownership group will take it.

How serious is the fire risk, honestly? Serious, current and central to the decision. Malibu has experienced two major fire events in recent memory — the 2018 Woolsey Fire, which burned to the sea and destroyed a great many structures, and a January 2025 fire that burned from the Palisades area into eastern Malibu. Risk varies enormously by parcel: canyon and hillside positions carry materially more exposure than an oceanfront lot. Insurance is expensive and in places difficult to obtain. We check the position on every home we list, and where we cannot get comfortable we do not list the home.

Can we get insurance? That is the right question and it should be answered before you commit rather than after. The Californian market for high-fire-risk areas has been difficult, with carriers withdrawing and the state's insurer of last resort taking on a larger role. Cover must be confirmed in writing for the specific property during the contingency period. In some Malibu purchases, availability rather than price is the binding constraint.

What happens when the highway closes? You wait, or you take a canyon road over the mountains, which is slow. There is no other answer, and it is one of the two structural facts about living here. In practice closures are usually hours rather than days, but after a fire, winter debris flows can close sections for longer. Build a margin into anything time-critical.

Is it walkable? No. Malibu has no town centre and the highway runs between most houses and most beaches. Each commercial cluster is walkable within itself; nothing else is. A car is essential and this is a driving-and-house destination rather than a strolling one.

When is it best? September and October, comfortably — warmest water, empty beaches, clear air and the best light of the year. April for the green hills and wildflowers. January for whales and solitude. July and August are the busiest and, because of the crowds and the traffic, not the best.

Which stretch should we choose? Beachfront if the ocean at the bottom of the steps is the entire point and the costs are acceptable. Point Dume for a settled bluff-top neighbourhood with beach access rights. The hillsides for the views. The canyons for value, seclusion and trails — with the fire question weighing heaviest there. West Malibu and Trancas for space and quiet at the cost of distance. Tell us how your household actually spends a week and we will point you at the right homes below.

Can we let our weeks? Where managed letting of unused weeks is provided for, it is handled by the management team rather than by you — but the City of Malibu regulates short-term rentals with a permit regime and rules that have been the subject of considerable local debate and change. The position must be checked for the specific property; we will tell you exactly what applies before you commit.

What are the running costs like? Higher than anywhere else on our list, and the insurance line is the reason. Each owner carries their share of the home's costs, billed transparently — property taxes, insurance, utilities, landscaping and brush clearance, wastewater and systems maintenance, cleaning, maintenance and the furnishing reserve. California's property tax reassessment on purchase is a further real line item. You see the full breakdown before you commit, not after, and in Malibu we would encourage you to read it twice.

Is the beach really public? Yes, below the mean high tide line, under California law — including in front of private houses. There have been long-running disputes on this coast about blocked access paths and signage, and the state has pursued them. As an owner it is worth understanding as a settled feature of ownership here rather than a grievance.

What should we do on a viewing trip? Come for three days, ideally in autumn. Drive the whole highway from the county line to Santa Monica and back so you understand the distances. Walk a canyon in the morning and a beach at sunset. Stand on the property at nine at night and listen to the road. Then ask us two questions before anything else — what does this house cost to insure, and what is its fire exposure — because in Malibu those answers shape everything. Three days answers more than three months of listings, and we will build the itinerary around the homes listed below.

Malibu sind vierunddreißig Kilometer Küste und praktisch eine einzige Straße. Der Pacific Coast Highway zieht sich über die ganze Länge, der Ozean auf der einen Seite, die steil aufsteigenden Santa Monica Mountains auf der anderen — und alles Weitere folgt aus dieser Geometrie: die Häuser, die Strände, die Canyons, der Verkehr, die Brände. Es gibt kein Ortszentrum, sondern eine Kette von Stränden, Canyons, Buchten und kleinen Geschäftsclustern zwischen Santa Monica und der Grenze zu Ventura County.

Das ergibt eine der schönsten Wohnküsten der Welt — und eine der am stärksten begrenzten. Dahinter sind die Berge fast vollständig geschützt; davor unterliegt die Küste einem der strengsten Küstenplanungsregime der USA. Das Wohnungsangebot ist im Kern fixiert — eine Stunde von achtzehn Millionen Menschen entfernt. Los Angeles liegt fünfundvierzig Minuten östlich.

sections.h: Waldbrandrisiko und Versicherung: der ehrliche Teil
p: Das ist das Wichtigste, was Sie vor einem Kauf hier wissen sollten — und kein Exposé wird es Ihnen sagen. Malibu liegt an der Schnittstelle von Siedlung und Wildland, mit trockenen Fallwinden im Herbst, und es brennt. Das Woolsey-Feuer im November 2018 reichte bis ans Meer und zerstörte sehr viele Gebäude; im Januar 2025 griff ein Feuer aus dem Gebiet Palisades auf den Osten Malibus über und zerstörte Häuser an der Küste. Das sind keine fernen Ereignisse, sondern die jüngste Erfahrung dieser Küste.

Die praktischen Folgen sind dauerhaft. Der kalifornische Versicherungsmarkt in Hochrisikogebieten ist teuer und selektiv geworden; teils ist nicht der Preis, sondern die Verfügbarkeit des Versicherungsschutzes die eigentliche Kaufhürde. Der Schutz muss vor jeder Verpflichtung schriftlich für das konkrete Objekt bestätigt werden. Hinzu kommen die gesetzliche Brandschutzpflege, Bauvorschriften, die Risiko und Versicherbarkeit stark verändern, sowie Schlammlawinen an verbrannten Hängen bei den folgenden Regenfällen. Wir prüfen das bei jedem Objekt, das wir listen.

sections.h: Miteigentum in Malibu, in der Praxis
p: Sie erwerben einen beurkundeten Bruchteil an einem konkreten, vollständig eingerichteten und professionell verwalteten Haus: echtes, auf Ihren Namen eingetragenes Eigentum, das Sie verkaufen, vererben oder halten können. Der Kalender verteilt die Nutzung fair und lässt die begehrtesten Termine — die Sommerwochen, Thanksgiving, Weihnachten und das besonders geschätzte Fenster im September und Oktober — von Jahr zu Jahr rotieren, mit flexibler Buchung für alles Übrige.

Das wirtschaftliche Argument ist hier besonders klar, und zwar nicht nur beim Kaufpreis: Die laufenden Kosten eines Hauses an dieser Küste — allen voran die Versicherung, dazu die vorgeschriebene Vegetationspflege, die Wartung der Kleinkläranlage, Salzluftkorrosion und die Vorbereitung auf die Brandsaison — sind hoch und steigen, und ein einzelner Haushalt trägt sie vollständig für ein Haus, das er sechs bis acht Wochen im Jahr nutzt. Teilen verteilt genau jene Kosten, die Malibu schwierig machen. Wir empfehlen ausdrücklich unabhängige rechtliche und steuerliche Beratung.

Malibu, ce sont trente-quatre kilomètres de côte et, en pratique, une seule route. La Pacific Coast Highway la parcourt d'un bout à l'autre, l'océan d'un côté et les montagnes de Santa Monica se dressant de l'autre, et toute la suite en découle : les maisons, les plages, les canyons, la circulation, les incendies. Il n'y a pas de centre-ville : une succession de plages, de canyons, de criques et de petits pôles commerciaux entre Santa Monica et la limite du comté de Ventura.

Il en résulte l'une des côtes résidentielles les plus belles au monde et l'une des plus contraintes. Derrière, les montagnes sont presque entièrement protégées ; devant, le littoral relève de l'un des régimes de planification côtière les plus stricts des États-Unis. L'offre de logements est pour l'essentiel figée — à une heure de dix-huit millions de personnes. Los Angeles est à quarante-cinq minutes à l'est.

sections.h: Risque d'incendie et assurance : la partie honnête
p: C'est le point le plus important à connaître avant d'acheter ici, et aucune annonce ne vous le dira. Malibu se trouve à l'interface entre urbanisation et espaces naturels, avec des vents de terre secs à l'automne, et elle brûle. L'incendie de Woolsey en novembre 2018 est descendu jusqu'à la mer et a détruit un très grand nombre de constructions ; en janvier 2025, un incendie parti du secteur de Palisades a gagné l'est de Malibu et détruit des maisons en bord de côte. Ce ne sont pas des épisodes lointains : c'est l'expérience récente de cette côte.

Les conséquences pratiques sont continues. Le marché californien de l'assurance en zone à haut risque est devenu cher et sélectif, et dans certains cas c'est la disponibilité de la couverture — et non son prix — qui conditionne l'achat. La couverture doit être confirmée par écrit pour le bien précis avant tout engagement. S'y ajoutent le débroussaillage réglementaire, des normes de construction qui changent fortement le risque et l'assurabilité, et les coulées de boue sur les versants brûlés lors des pluies suivantes. Nous le vérifions pour chaque bien publié.

sections.h: La copropriété à Malibu, en pratique
p: Vous achetez une fraction notariée d'une maison précise, entièrement meublée et gérée par des professionnels : une propriété réelle, enregistrée à votre nom, que vous pouvez vendre, transmettre ou conserver. Le calendrier répartit l'usage équitablement et fait tourner d'une année sur l'autre les dates les plus convoitées — les semaines d'été, Thanksgiving, Noël et la précieuse fenêtre de septembre-octobre —, avec réservation souple pour le reste.

L'argument économique est ici particulièrement net, et pas seulement à l'achat : les charges récurrentes d'une maison sur cette côte — l'assurance avant tout, plus le débroussaillage obligatoire, l'entretien de l'assainissement autonome, la corrosion saline et la préparation à la saison des incendies — sont élevées et croissantes, et un seul foyer les supporte entièrement pour une maison utilisée six à huit semaines par an. Le partage répartit précisément ce qui rend Malibu difficile. Nous vous encourageons toujours à prendre un conseil juridique et fiscal indépendant.

Malibú son treinta y cuatro kilómetros de costa y, en la práctica, una sola carretera. La Pacific Coast Highway la recorre entera, con el océano a un lado y las montañas de Santa Mónica levantándose al otro, y de esa geometría se deriva todo: las casas, las playas, los cañones, el tráfico y los incendios. No hay centro urbano: hay una sucesión de playas, cañones, calas y pequeños núcleos comerciales entre Santa Mónica y el límite del condado de Ventura.

El resultado es una de las costas residenciales más bellas del mundo y una de las más limitadas. Detrás, las montañas son casi por completo parque natural protegido; delante, la costa está regulada por uno de los regímenes de planeamiento litoral más estrictos de Estados Unidos. La oferta de vivienda es, en esencia, fija — a una hora de dieciocho millones de personas. Los Ángeles queda a cuarenta y cinco minutos hacia el este.

sections.h: Riesgo de incendio y seguro: la parte honesta
p: Es lo más importante que debe saber antes de comprar aquí, y ningún anuncio se lo dirá. Malibú se sitúa en la interfaz urbano-forestal, con vientos secos de tierra en otoño, y arde. El incendio Woolsey de noviembre de 2018 llegó hasta el mar y destruyó un gran número de edificaciones; en enero de 2025 un incendio en la zona de Palisades avanzó hacia el este de Malibú y destruyó viviendas junto a la costa. No son episodios lejanos: son la experiencia reciente de esta costa.

Las consecuencias prácticas son continuas. El mercado asegurador californiano en zonas de alto riesgo se ha encarecido y endurecido, y en algunos casos la disponibilidad de cobertura —no su precio— es el verdadero condicionante de la compra. La cobertura debe confirmarse por escrito para el inmueble concreto antes de comprometerse. Además: mantenimiento obligatorio del perímetro cortafuegos, estándares constructivos específicos que cambian mucho el riesgo y la asegurabilidad, y coladas de barro sobre laderas quemadas en las lluvias siguientes. Lo verificamos en cada vivienda que publicamos.

sections.h: Copropiedad en Malibú, en la práctica
p: Se adquiere una fracción escriturada de una casa concreta, amueblada y gestionada profesionalmente: propiedad real, inscrita a su nombre, que puede vender, transmitir o conservar. El calendario reparte el uso de forma equitativa y rota año a año las fechas más disputadas —las semanas de verano, Acción de Gracias, Navidad y el codiciado tramo de septiembre y octubre—, con reserva flexible para el resto.

Aquí el argumento económico es especialmente claro, y no solo por el precio de compra: los costes recurrentes de una casa en esta costa —seguro sobre todo, más desbroce obligatorio, mantenimiento de saneamiento autónomo, corrosión salina y preparación para la temporada de incendios— son altos y crecientes, y un solo hogar los soporta enteros para una casa que usa seis u ocho semanas al año. Compartir reparte precisamente los costes que hacen difícil a Malibú. Siempre recomendamos asesoramiento legal y fiscal independiente.
